In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the rejection of transplanted hearts into T. cruzi -infected mice is a parasite-specific reaction that occurs only in the presence of live parasites and that the absence of inflammation in transplanted hearts is due to the absence of live parasites.
T. cruzi does not induce an autoimmune rejection of heart transplants in the mouse model of Chagas disease.
the autoimmune rejection of transplanted heart tissue in experimental Chagas heart disease is a parasite specific response to infected host heart tissue and not a manifestation of the disease itself.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inflammatory response in Chagas disease is directed against the parasite and not the host tissue.
T. cruzi is a tissue-specific parasite that induces a parasite-specific response in its host.

the rejection of transplanted hearts is a parasite-specific reaction to the presence of parasites within the transplanted heart and that this response is similar to the rejection of native heart tissue.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the heart is not a target of autoimmune rejection in Chagas disease.

the inflammatory response to parasitized heart tissue in Chagas disease is parasite specific, not autoimmune, and therefore the inflammatory response to the parasite is not a result of an autoimmune response to host tissue.
T. cruzi is not an innocent bystander in the inflammatory response observed in the heart of infected individuals but rather a key player in the pathogenesis of the disease.
